1.pericope_label: The three at Mamre, and Abraham’s hospitality

schools.summary: Gill reads the visit as following quickly on the circumcision and marking God's approval of Abraham's ready obedience, prefers the rendering that puts him at the oaks of Mamre in an oaken grove chosen for its shade, and notes that the butter was what Jarchi took for cream skimmed from the milk. Calvin is uncertain whether this is a fresh appearance or a return to earlier matter, prefers the former, and explains it as the renewed assistance the faith of the saints requires at intervals, possibly repeated for Sarah's sake; he explains that the narrative calls the visitors men because they were clothed in human bodies, so that Abraham receiving them as men might give real proof of charity, angels having no need of our services. He qualifies the hospitality in a way the others do not, arguing that a man who killed calves for every passing stranger would soon have emptied his house, so that Abraham honoured what he could see of these men's worth rather than entertaining all comers, yet he takes Abraham's words to mean the guests were led there by God's direction and concludes that brethren in need are sent to us. In the running of the master, the labour of the mistress and the promptness of the servants he finds a picture of domestic government that long discipline alone could produce, and he raises without settling the question whether the angels truly ate.

Henry finds in the scene more freedom and familiarity and less grandeur and majesty than in the earlier appearances, so that it resembles the visit the Son of God was in due time to make to the world; he takes Abraham's sitting in the tent door not as repose but as watching for an opportunity of doing good to travellers, there being perhaps no inns, and draws from it that we have most comfort of the good works to which we are most forward, and that God visits those in whom he has first raised the expectation of him.

Clarke corrects the English at the outset, since the men stood over against Abraham rather than beside him, or he would not have needed to run from the tent door to meet them, and notes that the title Abraham uses is one of respect and not the covenant name, since he did not yet know his guests' quality. He sets out the three refreshments in what he takes to be their deliberate order — water for the feet, shade, and only then food — giving a physiological reason for the last coming last, since eating immediately after exertion hinders digestion and breeds fever; he observes that in those days a traveller reckoned he had a right to refreshment at the first tent he came to; he reckons the measures of meal at more than two bushels and quotes Fleury's inference that men of that age must have been great eaters, probably of larger stature and longer lives than ours; and he remarks that guests are still fed under trees in the East, feasts being scarcely ever held indoors. Wesley follows Henry on the familiarity of the appearance and on the purpose of sitting in the tent door, leaves open whether all three were created angels or one was the Son, and observes that religion does not destroy but improves good manners.

Ellicott denies that a new section could begin in this way, notes that a Jehovistic passage is here joined as closely as possible to an Elohistic one, and reports the Jewish tradition that the visit fell on the third day after the circumcision and was partly meant to heal Abraham, which would explain his resting at home instead of being with his herds. He gives the Jewish explanation of the number three, that no angel executes two commissions, but prefers to make one the angel of Jehovah and the other two his companions; he grants that the number has been taken to point at the Trinity and is read in church on Trinity Sunday, then warns expressly against pressing it as proof, lest anyone infer a personal appearance of the Father and the Spirit. He finds in Abraham's address only ordinary respect, the bowing being what an Arab sheikh would still do to a passing traveller, and notes the shift from singular to plural lest the companions seem unwelcome; he explains the washing of feet as cooling the whole body rather than merely removing dirt; and he accounts for the quantity of food by the customs of the tent, a wealthy sheikh's ordinary meal being flour and camels' milk, flesh seldom eaten and a kid killed only for a person of distinction, so that the calf marks guests of high rank and the bulk suggests numerous attendants. Keil and Delitzsch read the visit as an honour granted to a man newly received into covenant, name the visitors outright as Jehovah and two angels in human form, and give the appearance a double purpose, to establish Sarah's faith and to announce the judgment on Sodom.

debates: Why so much food was prepared. Clarke, following Fleury, infers that men of that age were great eaters and probably of larger stature and longer lives; Ellicott explains the same quantity by the customs of the tent, taking the calf as a mark of guests of high rank and the bulk as evidence that the three travelled with numerous attendants.

Who the three visitors were. Keil and Delitzsch name them as Jehovah and two angels; Ellicott reports the Jewish division of three commissions but prefers one angel of Jehovah with two companions, and cautions against using the number as proof of the Trinity; Wesley leaves it open between three created angels and one being the Son.

Whether the hospitality was indiscriminate. Calvin argues that it was not, since a man killing calves for all comers would have ruined himself, so that Abraham honoured the visible worth of these particular guests; Clarke and Ellicott treat the reception as the ordinary duty of a sheikh toward any traveller who reached his tent.
outliers: Ellicott's caution that the number three, though read in church on Trinity Sunday, must not be pressed as proof, lest it imply a personal appearance of the Father and the Spirit.
Clarke's physiological reason for the order of the refreshments, food coming last because eating straight after exertion hinders digestion.
The Jewish tradition Ellicott reports, that the visit came on the third day after circumcision and was partly to heal Abraham of its effects.
Fleury's inference, quoted by Clarke, that the bulk of meal shows the men of that age to have been larger and longer-lived than ours.

9.pericope_label: The promise of a son, and Sarah’s laughter

schools.summary: Gill denies that the question about Sarah sprang from ignorance, since one who knew her name knew where she was, and takes it as a way of drawing her to listen; he identifies the chief speaker as the Son of God in human form, hears in Sarah's laugh disbelief and perhaps derision, notes that the speaker did not turn toward her so that his knowledge should appear to come from omniscience rather than sight, and says plainly of her answer that it was a lie, to which she was tempted by the speaker's back being turned. Calvin explains the shifting of the speech, now to three and now to one, by saying that the three together represent one God while the chief place belongs to Christ, who often appeared to the fathers in an angel's form with angels for attendants; he attacks Jerome's rendering of the appointed term, I will return with life attending me, on the ground that God proclaiming his own power cannot borrow a form of speech supposing him mortal, and prefers to refer the phrase to the child rather than to Sarah's survival; he says Sarah foolishly set her own age against the word of God, adding that we reproach him whenever we measure his promises by the laws of nature; and he observes that God would have us reckon him present whenever he speaks through his ministers.

Henry explains why Sarah had to be within hearing though out of sight, since she was to conceive by faith and so the promise had to reach her, the modest usage of the time keeping women from eating with men and especially with strangers; he observes that by naming her the visitors gave Abraham intimation enough that, though they seemed strangers, they knew him and his family well.

Clarke allows two readings of the appointed term, either a full year or the nine months of an ordinary pregnancy, and reckons Abraham at ninety-nine when the promise was made; he holds that conception was now naturally impossible, so that a son must come supernaturally; he is gentler than the rest about the laugh, finding in it partly pleasure at the bare possibility and partly the smile of someone who thinks news too good to be true; he rests the identity of the speaker on the covenant name, which is never given to a created being, and infers the Angel of the covenant; and he notes that Luke adopts the Septuagint of the question about what is too hard almost word for word, turning it from a question into a statement. Wesley contrasts Sarah's laughter with Abraham's laughter of faith and calls hers one of doubting and distrust, and observes that she calls her husband lord, which the Holy Ghost notices to her honour.

Ellicott notes that the question about Sarah breached eastern manners, women being named only indirectly, and suspects Abraham had begun to see something more than human in his guests. On the appointed term he dismisses next spring as remote from eastern thought and one modern rendering as poetical but meaningless, preferring a year hence, since a year dies and a new one lives in its place, with Jewish tradition making the season the Passover; he also prefers the Greek reading which puts the tent door behind Sarah rather than behind the speaker. He defends Sarah at length, holding that her conduct has been very unjustly condemned, since Abraham may have guessed who the visitors were but she had no such suspicion, catching only fragments from within the tent and laughing at what she took for strangers ignorant of her age, and he glosses the word for waxing old as meaning worn out like a garment. He marks the moment of disclosure precisely, holding that only now is it made evident the travellers are from God, and that although the angel claims no divinity the narrator prefixes the covenant name to his words; and he reads Sarah's denial as the inconsistency of fright, a frightened woman taking refuge in falsehood and then, gently reproved, having her faith built up.

debates: How far Sarah is to be blamed for laughing. Gill hears derision, Wesley calls it doubting and distrust as against Abraham's laughter of faith, and Calvin says she set her own age against the word of God; Clarke softens it to the smile of one who thinks news too good to be true; Ellicott holds the condemnation very unjust, since she had no reason to suspect who the speakers were.

What the appointed term means. Clarke allows either a full year or nine months; Ellicott rejects next spring as un-eastern and one modern rendering as meaningless, preferring a year hence and reporting a tradition that fixes the season at Passover; Calvin rejects Jerome's rendering outright as making God speak like a mortal.
Whose life the phrase measures. Calvin reports the opinion that it refers to Sarah surviving until that date, and himself prefers to refer it to the child that was to be born.
outliers: Ellicott's defence of Sarah as catching only fragments from inside the tent and laughing at what she took for strangers ignorant of her age.
Calvin's refusal of Jerome's rendering on the ground that it would make God borrow a mortal's way of speaking about his own return.
Clarke's note that Luke adopts the Greek of this verse almost word for word, turning the question into a statement.
Ellicott's gloss that the Hebrew for waxing old means worn out like an old garment.
themes: a question asked to be overheard

16.pericope_label: Toward Sodom, and the counsel disclosed to Abraham

schools.summary: Gill leaves open whether the words about hiding were spoken to Abraham, to the two angels, or within the Godhead itself, and takes the knowing of Abraham for something warmer than omniscience, a special knowledge carrying love with it, as Jarchi also says; he has the Son of God in human form proposing to go down from higher ground to the plain where the cities stood. Calvin denies that Abraham's escort was courtesy at all, making it an honour rendered to angels, and cautions that the bodies they wore were temporary and not assumed as Christ assumed our nature; he agrees that the deliberation is for our sake, God having already determined what he would do, and finds two reasons for the disclosure, the privilege Abraham already held and the profit it would bring posterity, in which he sees the whole scope and use of revelation. He holds that Abraham was admitted to the counsel because he would faithfully instruct his own family, since God does not make his will known that the knowledge may perish with us; and he observes that the iniquities are set out before the punishment is named, since otherwise the history would not instruct, adding that the delay commends God's moderation, who does not fulminate at once but strikes only when the case is desperate, though we always think ourselves used more severely than is just.

Henry marks the turn from mercy to judgment, the guests setting their faces toward Sodom in wrath as God is said to have looked upon the host of the Egyptians, and observes that though God has long seemed to connive at sinners, from which they infer that he does not see or regard, he will look toward them when the day of his wrath comes.

Clarke sees in Abraham's walking with the visitors one more piece of primitive hospitality, since there were no public roads and a guide was a necessity; he reads the question about hiding as a common scriptural idiom, a question asked where an affirmative is meant; he glosses the way of the Lord as true religion, to be kept not only in the creed but in the practice; and he turns the going down into a lesson for magistrates, who should not judge upon report but inquire accurately into the facts. Wesley takes the deliberation as God expressing himself after the manner of men, and draws from it that those who live in communion with him know more of his mind than others; he calls Abraham's instruction of his household a bright part of his character, making him prophet and king as well as priest in his own house with catechized servants, and turning it into a charge on masters to inspect the manners of everyone under their roof; and he insists that God is in no doubt when he says he will go down.

Ellicott notes the strange mingling of human and divine that persists even after the disclosure, the visitors still called men and Abraham still doing a host's duty, and reports the tradition that he went as far as a village from which the Dead Sea can be seen down a ravine. On the clause about knowing Abraham he allows that most versions support the received rendering, which makes Abraham's good conduct earn the divine condescension, but insists the Hebrew says rather that God had known him in order that he might command his sons, so that the purpose for which he was called, and not his merit, is the reason he is told. He holds that God examines before he punishes with the care of the most conscientious earthly judge, reports the reading which takes the disputed word as a noun and would turn the clause into a sentence of utter destruction, finds its ellipse harsh, and keeps the adverb on the ground that inquiry rather than punishment is the prominent thought — the two angels going to give Sodom a final trial which upright treatment would have passed. Keil and Delitzsch explain the cry of Sodom as an appeal for vengeance that ascends to heaven, and take the disputed word as a noun on the evidence of Isaiah rather than as an adverb; they note that the men turned thence toward Sodom while Abraham remained standing before Jehovah.

debates: How the clause about knowing Abraham should be rendered. Ellicott grants that most versions favour the received sense, in which Abraham's conduct earns the condescension, but argues from the Hebrew that God had known him in order that he might command his household, making the purpose of his calling the reason; Gill glosses the knowing as a special knowledge carrying love; Calvin and Wesley build on the received sense and make the instruction of the household the ground.

Whether the disputed word is an adverb or a noun. Keil and Delitzsch declare it a noun on the evidence of Isaiah, which would make the clause a sentence of utter destruction; Ellicott reports that reading, objects that the ellipse it requires is harsh, and keeps the adverb, since inquiry and not punishment is the prominent thought.

What is meant by God going down to see. Wesley says he is in no doubt and speaks after the manner of men; Calvin makes it a commendation of divine moderation, punishment coming only when the case is desperate; Clarke turns it into a lesson to magistrates against judging on report; Ellicott treats it as a real final trial which Sodom might have passed.
outliers: Ellicott's report of the tradition placing Abraham's escort as far as a village from which the Dead Sea can be seen down a ravine.
Wesley's description of Abraham as prophet and king as well as priest in his own house, with catechized servants.
Clarke's use of the verse as a lesson to magistrates, not to judge according to report but to inquire into the facts.
Ellicott's reading that the two angels went to give Sodom a final trial, so that upright treatment of them would have spared the city.
themes: shall I hide it from Abraham
a judge who goes down to see

schools.summary: Gill has Abraham drawing nigh in prayer, citing the Targum that he prayed, and notes the mixture of faith, freedom and holy boldness with a deep sense of his own meanness and unworthiness; he accounts for the first figure by the five cities of the plain with ten righteous supposed for each, represents the plea as urging that the thing would be unbecoming the divine Majesty, has Abraham fearing to weary a superior by importunity, and observes at the close that it is an act of sovereignty how long God will commune with a creature, unbroken communion not being for this life. Calvin denies that Abraham teaches God his duty as one might remind a judge what his office requires, insisting that he reasons instead from God's nature, whose will is itself the law of justice and rectitude, and granting that the impious use the same form of speech in murmuring while Abraham does something wholly different with it. He faces the harder fact that when God chastises a people the good are often carried off with the reprobate, as Daniel and Ezekiel and Ezra were swept into exile, and answers that we must look to the end, since a husbandman who can sort grain from chaff is not to be thought abler than his Maker; and on the confession of dust and ashes he observes that the nearer Abraham comes to God the more abject he knows himself, only that brightness stripping a man of his intoxicated self-confidence.

Henry makes the intercession grow straight out of the revelation, since communion is kept up by word and prayer together and God's word does us good when it furnishes matter for asking and stirs us to it. In the phrase about drawing near he finds two things, a holy concern that asks whether Sodom shall be destroyed without one good word spoken for it, and a holy confidence that approaches as a prince, with the assurance of faith.

Clarke reads the opening plea as a principle rather than a request, that the righteous are not punished for the crimes of the impious, and asks who can pray with hope who cannot give God and his own conscience a reason for what he asks; he holds that God alone is judge of all men and that Abraham addresses the person before him either as the Supreme Being or as his representative; he notes that dust and ashes are close in sound because close in kind, the lightest particles of earth and the residue of what has been burnt, and draws the moral that high thoughts of oneself go with low thoughts of God. He explains the stopping point by Lot's household professing the true religion, so that ten seemed a safe number, and observes that the presence remained as long as the praying continued, the glory being lifted up only when Abraham ceased. Wesley repeats Henry on the drawing near, remarks that God is pleased when he is wrestled with though a man so importuned would be angry, offers two reasons for the pleading stopping where it did, and adds that we are worms of the earth while he is the Lord of glory.

Ellicott observes that Jewish commentators find the verb used especially of prayer and calls the intercession unspeakably noble; he defends Abraham's motive, denying that he thought only of Lot, since he had once restored their people and goods to the king of Sodom, had seen their affection as parent met child and friend met friend, and hoped such a deliverance had left some good among them. He also denies that the descending numbers were a device, refusing to let Abraham begin high in order to come down, and holding that it was the readiness with which each request was granted that drew him on, so that the passage illustrates how a believer's faith grows by being answered. On the departure he gives a reason of his own, not the avoiding of importunity, since Abraham had finished and had been granted all he asked, but the fulfilment of the revelation's purpose — to show the justice of God's dealings and, beyond that, that the Gentile world lay under his dominion and within reach of his mercy, the lesson the book of Jonah would teach later.

debates: Why Abraham stopped at ten. Wesley offers two reasons, that he owned the place deserved to perish if it could not furnish so many, or that God restrained his spirit from asking further; Clarke supplies a third, that Lot's household professed the true religion so that ten seemed a safe number and further urging appeared needless.

Whether the descending numbers were a device. Ellicott denies it flatly, refusing to let Abraham begin high with the intention of coming down, and makes the readiness of each answer the thing that drew him on; the others treat the sequence simply as importunity, Gill having him fear to weary a superior.

Whether the righteous perish with the wicked. Clarke lays it down as an invariable principle of justice that they do not, and makes this the foundation of the whole supplication; Calvin grants that in national chastisements they often are swept away together, instancing the exile, and directs attention to the end, which discriminates them.
outliers: Ellicott's suggestion that Abraham hoped for good people in Sodom because he had once seen their human affection when he restored their captives to them.
Clarke's observation that the presence of God remained while Abraham prayed and was lifted up only when he ceased.
Wesley's remark that God is pleased when he is wrestled with, though a man importuned in the same way could not but be angry.
Ellicott's conclusion that the episode showed the Gentile world both subject to God's dominion and within reach of his mercy, as the book of Jonah would afterwards teach.
themes: the Judge of all the earth
